content: The insertion of central venous catheters (CVCs) is associated with a risk of bleeding during and after the procedure. Patients requiring a central line often have coagulation abnormalities due to their underlying medical conditions, co-existing illnesses, or the effects of treatments they are undergoing. In some clinical settings, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is prophylactically transfused to correct clotting factor deficiencies and reduce the risk of bleeding before central line placement. However, FFP transfusion carries its own risks, and it is unclear whether this practice effectively reduces bleeding or improves other clinically significant outcomes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of different prophylactic plasma transfusion regimens administered prior to central line insertion in patients with abnormal coagulation. To achieve this, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were searched in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, and the Transfusion Evidence Library, up to March 1, 2016. Only RCTs published in English that involved plasma transfusions to prevent bleeding in patients of any age with abnormal coagulation requiring CVC insertion were included. Four trials were identified as eligible for inclusion, but three of these trials are still ongoing. The single included study randomized 81 adults in intensive care with an International Normalized Ratio (INR) of ≥1.5 to either receive no FFP or a single dose of 12 mL/kg FFP prior to undergoing central venous catheterization (58 participants) or other invasive procedures (23 participants). For this review, only the subgroup of 58 adults undergoing CVC insertion was analyzed. The study authors provided unpublished data for the outcomes relevant to this review. The quality of the evidence was assessed as low or very low across different outcomes using the GRADE methodology. The included study had a high risk of bias due to the lack of blinding of participants and personnel, as well as an imbalance in the number of participants with liver disease between the study groups. There was insufficient evidence to determine whether FFP reduced the risk of major bleeding related to the procedure within 24 hours, as no major bleeding events occurred in either study arm (very low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was significant uncertainty regarding whether FFP reduced minor bleeding within 24 hours, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.67 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.12 to 3.70, very low-quality evidence). No studies were identified that evaluated other important outcomes, such as all-cause mortality, the proportion of participants receiving plasma or red blood cell transfusions, serious adverse reactions (e.g., transfusion-related or line-related complications), length of hospital stay, changes in INR, or quality of life. The three ongoing studies are still recruiting participants, with a combined expected enrollment of up to 355 participants, and are anticipated to be completed by February 2018. However, these studies are small and do not address all the comparisons included in this review. Therefore, they are unlikely to provide definitive answers to the review’s questions. In conclusion, there is very limited evidence from one RCT to guide the decision on whether or not to administer prophylactic plasma transfusion prior to central venous catheterization in patients with abnormal coagulation. Based on the current evidence, it is not possible to determine whether prophylactic plasma transfusion is beneficial or harmful in this context. To detect a clinically meaningful increase in the proportion of participants experiencing major bleeding (e.g., from 1% to 2%), a much larger study with at least 4,634 participants would be required (80% power, 5% significance level).
